newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Analysts look to Boonstra for new Philips strategy.
newsitem.headline: Analysts look to Boonstra for new Philips strategy.

text.p: When Cor Boonstra takes the reins at Philips Electronics NV on Tuesday analysts will be looking for signs he can blow away the perception of Europe's biggest consumer electronics firm as a lumbering, unfocused giant.
Analysts say Boonstra needs new strategies to build on the achievements of outgoing chairman Jan Timmer, who dragged Philips from the brink of financial disaster in the early 1990s.
Boonstra, with a track record of vigorous restructuring, might take an axe to costs but that may not be enough to convince analysts Philips has a winning formula for the future.

"The main question in my view is does he have any different strategic views? Will he look beyond cost cutting to find new growth areas apart from Asia, also maybe (find) new activities or new alliances?" said Joost van Beek of Van Meer James Capel.
"Strategy," said Van Beek. "That's what I'm most curious about. I'm not interested in cost-cutting."
"It's very clear in this market that if you want to win you have to include alliances, like in the DVD (digital video disc) area where you have to find compromises," he added.

Analysts agree Philips is no longer the slow-moving unprofitable leviathan of the early 1990s, with more clearly defined management structures and a commitment to developing and delivering goods consumers want.

But does the company now need a a re-run of Timmer's Centurion plan, which hauled Philips from losses of 4.2 billion guilders in 1990 to 1995's profit of 2.5 billion guilders and shed 60,000 jobs from Philips' then 310,000 payroll?
Analysts say they want more.
London-based Morgan Stanley analyst Angela Dean called for a more sharper focus.
"Philips needs to sharpen up a bit, in general terms, on non-performing businesses and maybe in marketing terms," Dean said.

"The whole idea of getting businesses to perform the way they should, finding clear growth areas, setting clear strategies and enhancing shareholder value, those are the kind of things people are looking for," she said.
Philips insiders say 58-year old Boonstra, the son of a grocery store owner from the northern Dutch province of Friesland, is fiercely committed to value for shareholders.

"He is a man who expects people to live up to their commitments, to produce what they say they will -- that's how he does things," said a Philips source, requesting anonimity. "I also think he's in a bit of a hurry to get results."
Boonstra worked for Unilever and headed the U.S. Sara Lee Corp before joining Philips in 1994.

"He's not a Philips man. Maybe it brings a fresh approach. He's come from a background at Sara Lee that's strong on brand names, pretty good on restructuring -- all things that are relevant for Philips," Morgan Stanley's Dean said.
"His main strength is that he has a fresh view because he comes from outside. That's unique, he's the very first chairman from outside," Van Beek said.
"Another major strength is that he was bred in marketing-related jobs. That's still one of their (Philips) weaker spots although this has improved," he added.
But if Boonstra is to shake up perceptions of Philips and galvanise the share price back to the 83.90 guilder high of last year, he has to find new markets and approaches.

Alliances and cooperations are vital in opening up new market as technologies such as DVD and opportunities on the InterNet unfold. DVDs are high capacity storage discs which can hold feature length movies.

Philips was bruised badly in the 1980s as it lost out in a video recorder standard battle with the Japanese, and it can not afford to strike off on its own with new developments such as its Digital Compact Cassette or CD-Interactive, analysts said.

"It's not something you can force, but what I need is the feeling that he's willing to look for more compromise over alliances to make sure that new products are established," said Van Meer James Capel's Van Beek.
